pack.title: Three checks on a historical document

provenance.notes: The three checks are this pack's own organising scheme, named and defined here so that every question turns on the supplied definitions rather than on remembered terminology. Text-only pack, matching the structure of the text-only official exercise.

blocks.text: Three checks on a historical document

Before a historian relies on what a document says, three separate checks are applied to it. This text calls them the attribution check, the proximity check and the interest check. They are independent of one another: a document may pass one and fail another, and each has to be applied on its own rather than blurred into a single impression of how trustworthy the document feels.

The attribution check asks whether the document is what it presents itself as being: whether it was written by the person named in it, at the time and in the place it claims. Physical evidence such as the material the document is written on can settle this check on its own. A document that fails it is not thereby worthless, but any statement whose force depends on the claimed origin must be set aside.

The proximity check asks how close the author stood to what is described. An author who saw an event is closer to it than one who was told of it by a participant, and both are closer than a compiler assembling an account several generations later. Proximity concerns the route by which the information reached the author, and says nothing about whether the author is honest.

The interest check asks what the author stood to gain or lose if the account were believed. An author with something at stake may still report accurately, so a failed interest check is not a finding of falsehood. It obliges the historian to record the stake and to look for confirmation from somewhere else. Interest concerns motive, and is unaffected by how near the author stood to the events.

Two accounts confirm one another only when they are independent, meaning that neither is derived from the other and both do not descend from a common earlier account. Where several surviving texts all descend from one lost original, their agreement establishes only that the copying was faithful. The number of surviving copies makes no difference to this.

A document that fails one of the checks may still be valuable, provided the historian's question does not depend on what the failed check governs. A charter forged long after the date it claims is worthless as evidence for the transactions it records, but it is direct evidence for the concerns of the period in which the forgery was actually made.

questions.stem: According to the text, what does the proximity check concern?

options.text: How soon after the events described the document was written down.
The route by which the information reached the author.
How much detail the author gives about what is described.
Whether the author reported honestly what he believed to be true.

supportSpans.quote: Proximity concerns the route by which the information reached the author

questions.explanation: The text defines proximity as how close the author stood to what is described, and spells out that this is a matter of the route the information took: seeing an event, being told of it by a participant, or compiling it generations later.

a.reason: Delay is suggestive but is not what the text measures. A witness writing forty years later still saw the event; a contemporary who only heard a rumour did not.

c.reason: The text says nothing about how much detail an account gives. Detail can be invented as easily as it can be remembered.

d.reason: The text closes the paragraph by saying the opposite: proximity says nothing about whether the author is honest.

hints.text: The paragraph on proximity ends by ruling one common answer out explicitly.
It describes a chain: seeing something, being told of it, compiling it much later.
What the check measures is how the information travelled, not when it arrived or how honest the teller was.

questions.stem: A letter bears the signature of a city official and the date 1421. Analysis shows that the paper it is written on was not manufactured before 1500. According to the text, what follows?

options.text: The letter is worthless, and nothing in it can be used.
Whatever the letter says that rests on its being a 1421 document by that official must be set aside.
The person who signed it must have had something to gain from the deception.
The date was miscopied by a later hand, so the letter can stand as it is.

supportSpans.quote: A document that fails it is not thereby worthless, but any statement whose force depends on the claimed origin must be set aside.

questions.explanation: The paper settles the question of origin on physical evidence alone: the letter cannot be what it presents itself as being. The text is precise about the consequence — not that the document is discarded, but that whatever it says which draws its force from the claimed authorship and date no longer stands.

a.reason: The text states directly that a document failing this check is not thereby worthless. What is lost is a class of statements, not the document.

c.reason: Motive is a separate matter, and the text keeps it separate. A false origin can be established without any finding about who benefited.

d.reason: A miscopied date would not put the letter on paper that did not yet exist. The text treats physical evidence as able to settle this check on its own.

hints.text: Decide first what the paper proves, and then read what the text says the consequence is.
The paragraph on this check ends with a careful sentence about what is lost and what is not.
The text distinguishes discarding a document from setting aside particular statements in it.

questions.stem: A monk compiled his account of a battle sixty years after it took place, drawing on stories circulating in his monastery. He belonged to no party to the conflict and gained nothing from how the battle was remembered. Which check is most directly at issue, and what is its outcome?

options.text: The interest check, which the account fails.
The proximity check, which the account fares poorly on.
The attribution check, which the account fails.
The proximity check, which the account passes.

supportSpans.quote: both are closer than a compiler assembling an account several generations later

questions.explanation: The monk is at the far end of the chain the text describes: not a witness, not told by a participant, but a compiler working from what was in circulation two generations on. That is what the proximity check measures, and the account stands poorly on it. Nothing here fails: the monk had no stake, and the account is what it claims to be.

a.reason: The check that concerns motive is not at issue. The monk belonged to no party and gained nothing by the account being believed, so there is no stake for it to find.

c.reason: Nothing suggests the account is other than what it presents itself as being. Writing long after the events is not a false claim about who wrote it or when.

d.reason: The check is the right one and the verdict is the wrong way round. A compiler working from circulating stories stands at the furthest of the positions the text sets out.

hints.text: Two of the details in the description bear on different checks; decide which of them the question is about.
The detail about the monk belonging to no party disposes of one check rather than raising it.
The text ranks three positions an author can occupy relative to what is described. Work out which one the monk occupies.

questions.stem: A set of household accounts is attributed to a well-known abbey steward, but was in fact drawn up by an assistant whose name is nowhere recorded. A historian is studying how households of this kind managed their supplies. According to the text, how should the accounts be treated?

options.text: As worthless, because a document that fails a check cannot serve as evidence.
As evidence for the steward's own practice, since an assistant would have worked to his instructions.
As sound evidence for this historian's question, which does not turn on who wrote the accounts.
As usable only once a second set of accounts from another household shows the same practice.

supportSpans.quote: A document that fails one of the checks may still be valuable, provided the historian
any statement whose force depends on the claimed origin must be set aside

questions.explanation: The accounts fail the attribution check: they are not by the person named in them. The text does not make that fatal. It makes the failed check fatal only to statements whose force depends on the claimed origin. How supplies were managed is recorded by the accounts whoever held the pen, so the historian's question is untouched by the failure.

a.reason: The text says explicitly that a document failing one of the checks may still be valuable. Failing a check narrows what a document can be used for; it does not discard it.

b.reason: This is the one use the failed check does rule out. Any statement about the steward himself depends on the claimed authorship, which is exactly what has been shown to be false.

d.reason: Corroboration is what the text asks for after a failed interest check, where motive is in doubt. Here the historian's question does not depend on the check that failed, so no second document is needed to license it.

hints.text: Work out which of the three checks these accounts fail before deciding what follows from it.
The text says a failed check rules out a particular kind of statement, not the document.
Ask whether what this historian wants to know depends on who wrote the accounts.

questions.stem: Two chronicles describe the same famine. The earlier was written by a monk who lived through it. The later was copied from the earlier a century afterwards, and adds one detail the earlier does not contain: the name of the official who organised relief. A historian asks how well that detail is attested. According to the text, what follows?

options.text: It is well attested, because two surviving accounts record the famine.
It rests on the later chronicle alone, which is derived from the earlier and cannot confirm it.
It is well attested, because the later chronicler worked from an account written by a witness.
It must be invented, because a detail absent from the earlier account cannot be genuine.

supportSpans.quote: Two accounts confirm one another only when they are independent, meaning that neither is derived from the other

questions.explanation: The later chronicle is copied from the earlier, so the two are not independent and their agreement about the famine confirms nothing. The disputed detail is a further problem: it appears in the derivative text alone, so there is only ever one account of it, and that account is the more distant of the two.

a.reason: Counting surviving accounts is precisely what the text rules out. Confirmation requires independence, and the number of copies makes no difference to it.

c.reason: Having a witness's account to hand improves what the later chronicler could copy accurately. It cannot vouch for a detail that the witness's account does not contain.

d.reason: The text draws no such conclusion. A detail resting on one late account is weakly attested, which is not the same as shown to be false.

hints.text: Ask first whether these two chronicles count as two accounts at all, in the sense the text requires.
The text sets a condition that two accounts must meet before either can confirm the other.
Then notice which of the two chronicles the disputed detail actually appears in.

questions.stem: A pamphlet carries the name of a printer whose workshop is known to have been operating in the year the pamphlet bears, and it describes a riot the printer says he watched from his own window. The printer was in the pay of the city council, which the pamphlet praises for restoring order. According to the text, how do the three checks stand?

options.text: All three pass.
Attribution and proximity pass; the interest check does not.
Attribution passes; the proximity and interest checks both fail.
All three fail.

supportSpans.quote: They are independent of one another: a document may pass one and fail another
The attribution check asks whether the document is what it presents itself as being
The interest check asks what the author stood to gain or lose if the account were believed.

questions.explanation: The workshop dates confirm the pamphlet is what it presents itself as being, so the first check passes. The printer describes what he saw himself, which is the closest position the text recognises, so the second passes. He was paid by the party the pamphlet praises and stood to gain if his account of its conduct were believed, so it is the third that fails. The text insists the three are applied separately, and here they come apart.

a.reason: Two of the three details settle two of the checks favourably. The third detail — who was paying the printer, and what the pamphlet says about them — is left unaccounted for.

c.reason: The text states that motive is unaffected by how near the author stood to the events. Being paid does not move an eyewitness further from what he saw.

d.reason: A failed check does not condemn a document outright, and it certainly does not carry the other two down with it. The text says a document may pass one and fail another.

hints.text: Take the three checks one at a time rather than forming a single impression of the pamphlet.
Each of the three details in the description bears on exactly one of them.
The text warns explicitly against letting one check carry another, in either direction.
